notes.1a: Although most candidates clearly understood what is meant by prime cost and work in progress very few were able to fully explain both terms.
notes.1b: The manufacturing account was prepared to a high standard by nearly all candidates with a significant number being awarded full marks. The most common error was the miscalculation of depreciation. Few candidates incorrectly deducted the indirect costs from the prime cost and lost
notes.1c: Responses were variable with some strong answers but also some which demonstrated a lack of understanding. Despite the question asking for reference to accounting concepts and calculations some candidates did not provide these.
notes.2a: A significant number of candidates did correctly calculate the profit and were awarded three marks. Some, however, completed partial calculations and submitted answers of $1080000 or $54000.
notes.2b: Performance varied with many candidates producing correct statements and being awarded twelve or more marks> However, some candidates prepared poor statements with incorrect figures often not supported by workings. The trade and other receivables figure was usually calculated correctly as was the cost of sales. Errors often occurred with the subsequent derivation of the closing inventory and/or trade and other payables. Marks were often lost for the retained earnings figure and invariably the workings were not shown so candidates could not be given any credit for an incorrect final figure.
notes.2c: Many candidates calculated the ratio correctly but some incorrectly provided their answer as a monetary value.
notes.2d: This part was not well answered. Many stated that the ratios were ‘higher’ or ‘lower’ but did not develop their answer as to whether this was better or worse for the company and some stated that a higher inventory turnover measured in days was beneficial.
notes.3a: Most candidates were able to identify a benefit of auditing but few were able to explain the benefit sufficiently to be awarded the second mark.
notes.3b: Most candidates correctly identified the required IAS for items 1 and 2 but relatively few could being able to explain the impairment loss and the non-adjusting event satisfactorily. However, explanations for item 3, with few exceptions, were not worthy of credit.
notes.3c: Few candidates calculated the revised retained earnings fully correctly but most made the majority of adjustments correctly. The most common errors were the incorrect treatment of the deposit and the goods sent to a customer on a sale or return basis.
notes.3d: This was not well answered and very few candidates included the cash and cash equivalents in the total assets figure.
notes.3e: Most candidates scored the available mark for providing the advice. Candidates generally attempted a justification but the explanations were lacking in substance and relatively few were awarded more than three of the five available marks.
notes.4a: Although most candidates identified the introduction of cash few made reference to the capital.
notes.4b: There were relatively few correct explanations with some believing that the transactions were at the cessation of the joint venture.
notes.4c: There were some correct solutions with common errors being the omission of the sale of the fixtures and/or the inclusion of the drawings.
notes.4d: There were very few fully correct ledger accounts with a range of errors including reversal of the entries and inclusion of total sales.
notes.4e: The mark for advice was generally awarded but then responses tended to be generic rather than scenario based.
notes.4f: Most candidates were awarded two marks for the profit/not for profit difference and some did develop their answer and were rewarded accordingly.
notes.5i: Some candidates were able to correctly calculate the net cash flow for each year. Where the flows were not correct the error was usually as a result of miscalculating the cost of sales.
notes.5ii: Most candidates were able to correctly calculate the payback period. Full credit was given for a correct calculation based on the candidate’s own figure where the cash flows were not correct. A limited number of candidates did not round up correctly.
notes.5iii: This was well answered with many fully correct answers. Marks were often lost for the incorrect treatment of depreciation and the failure to submit the answer to two decimal places as was clearly requested in the question paper.
notes.5b: This was generally well answered with most candidates were able to state two disadvantages and a few were able to state the required advantages.
notes.5c: This was very well answered with nearly all candidates able to calculate the net present value using either the correct figures or the candidate’s own figures.
notes.5d: Responses were acceptable with nearly all candidates gaining the available marks for the decision and for commenting on the net present value. Few gained the marks for comments on the payback period and accounting rate of return.
notes.6a: Most candidates gave acceptable responses and were awarded two marks.
notes.6b: Most candidates were awarded five marks but few were able to deal correctly with the semi- variable overheads and consequently the other three marks were lost. A limited number of candidates produced two budgets with one being based on 1 000 units and the other on 3 000
notes.6c: Most candidates made a reasonable attempt at the reconciliation. The most common errors were the incorrect calculation of the semi-variable overheads variance and the fixed costs variance.
notes.6d: Responses were generally satisfactory with most providing appropriate suggestions.
notes.6e: Most candidates were able to score three of the available five marks as they provided advice along with two advantages. Only a limited number of candidates provided any disadvantages but those that did were rewarded accordingly. ACCOUNTING
